title: Time course of loss of adaptations after stopping prolonged intense endurance training
authors: Coyle EF, Martin WH, Sinacore DR, Joyner MJ, Hagberg JM, Holloszy JO
population: Seven endurance-trained subjects studied 12, 21, 56 and 84 days after cessation of training, compared with eight sedentary control subjects (longitudinal detraining study, not a crossover)
findings: VO2max declined 7% during the first 21 days of inactivity and stabilised after 56 days at 16% below the initial trained value.
After 84 days of detraining the subjects still had a higher VO2max than eight sedentary controls (50.8 vs 43.3 ml/kg/min), mainly due to a larger arterial-mixed venous O2 difference.
Exercise stroke volume declined early to control levels; the initial VO2max decline related to reduced stroke volume and the later decline to reduced a-vO2 difference.

Citrate synthase and succinate dehydrogenase activities declined with a half-time of 12 days and stabilised 50% above sedentary controls; capillarization did not decline and remained 50% above sedentary.
limitations: Seven subjects with complete training cessation, 1980s methods, not run-specific, no retraining phase.
implications: Seed the layoff model with an early fast decline (about 7% VO2max by 3 weeks, about 16% by 8 weeks) that plateaus above the sedentary level; a 12-day half-time for oxidative enzyme loss supports reducing paces noticeably after 2-3 weeks off.
Bound modelled loss for long-trained runners at roughly 15-20% of VO2max rather than returning to zero; this is a 7-subject estimate and should be a default, not a fact for every runner.
